docs.title: What's the difference between a chatbot and an agent?
docs.text:
Autonomy. A chatbot is reactive. You send a message, it answers, it waits. You're driving every step.

An agent gets a goal, some tools, and a loop. It decides what to do, does it, looks at the result, and decides again until the task is done or it hits a stopping point. You give it the destination and it figures out the route.

docs.title: How does an agent actually use tools?
docs.text:
Through function calling (also called tool calling). The model can't run anything itself, it only outputs text. So the app hands it a list of tools with descriptions, the model replies with a structured request like "call search_signin_logs with these arguments," and the app is the one that actually runs it. The result goes back into the context window and the model keeps going.

The more an agent gets to pick its own tools and act without checking with you first, the more agentic it is.

On the Microsoft side, Microsoft Agent Framework is the SDK for building agents now. It's the successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen and it's made by the same teams.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: What is MCP?
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard Anthropic released in November 2024 for connecting AI apps to tools and data. Before MCP, every app needed its own custom integration for every tool. Now a tool gets wrapped as an MCP server once, and any MCP client (Claude Code, VS Code, Microsoft Foundry agents) can use it. Kind of like USB-C for AI tools.

The security catch is that an MCP server is just code running with whatever access you give it. A sketchy one can leak tokens or hide instructions in its tool descriptions (tool poisoning). OWASP has a whole MCP Top 10 for this.

Documentation | Model Context Protocol

Documentation | OWASP

docs.title: Why does this matter for security?
docs.text:
The agent loop (get goal, plan, act, check result, repeat) is what Security Copilot agents, Claude Code, and SOAR-style automations all run on. It's also the risk. An agent with tools can do real damage if it gets tricked, and that's exactly what prompt injection goes after (see AI Flaws). OWASP calls this LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency.

Microsoft's guidance lines up with what we'd do for any service account:

  • Least privilege: give the agent only the permissions it needs, and only for as long as it needs them.
  • Human in the loop: anything risky (deleting, sending, changing permissions) gets approved by a person first.
  • Logging: every tool call should be logged so you can actually investigate when something goes wrong.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: AI Flaws: Hallucinations and Prompt Injection
Why do models hallucinate, and what kinds of hallucinations are dangerous?
docs.text:
A hallucination is when the model says something wrong with full confidence. Not a typo. More like making up a citation, a CVE, or a PowerShell cmdlet that doesn't exist.

Part of what I first wrote is right. Training data has wrong stuff in it, and when the model doesn't have the answer it still answers anyway. The bigger reason is how LLMs work. They predict the most likely next token, not the true one. If a made-up answer fits the pattern better than "I don't know," the made-up answer wins.

Training also tends to reward guessing over admitting it doesn't know. It's like a multiple choice test where leaving it blank is a guaranteed zero but guessing might get you points. OpenAI's 2025 paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate" makes that argument.

The dangerous ones for security work:

  • Fake packages. The model suggests a pip or npm package that doesn't exist, and attackers register those names with malware in them ("slopsquatting"). Copy-paste the install command and you just ran their code. That's a supply chain attack (OWASP A03:2025).
  • Wrong queries and commands. KQL that runs fine but quietly misses events, so your detection has a blind spot you don't know about. Or an az command with the wrong flags.
  • Made-up CVEs and compliance requirements. Now you're remediating the wrong thing or giving an auditor the wrong answer.
  • Fake citations. Lawyers in Mata v. Avianca (2023) got sanctioned for filing a brief with court cases ChatGPT made up.

The scary hallucinations are the ones that look right and don't fail loudly. Check anything that matters against the real source (Microsoft Learn, NVD, the package registry) before you use it. OWASP lists this as LLM09:2025 Misinformation.

Tim and Moby Explains

docs.title: What is a system prompt and why is it not a security boundary?
docs.text:
A system prompt is the hidden message the app sends before your chat that sets the model's role, rules, and behavior. Something like "You're a SOC assistant. Only answer security questions."

What I got wrong

I originally wrote that a system prompt is "not instructions." It is instructions. The point is that nothing enforces them.

The system prompt is just text sitting in the same context window as everything else. The only thing making it work is the model choosing to follow it. No code checks it, and the model can't reliably tell the developer's instructions apart from the user's message or text inside a document. That means:

  1. It can be overridden. Good prompt injection can get the model to ignore it.
  2. It can leak. Users can often get the model to repeat it back, so never put secrets, API keys, or internal URLs in a system prompt.
  3. It's not access control. "Don't show salary data to non-HR users" in a system prompt doesn't stop anything. The app has to check permissions before the data ever gets to the model.

A system prompt is like an "Employees Only" sign on a door. The badge reader is the actual security boundary.

I also said this topic was too new to have much research. That's outdated. OWASP lists it as LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage, and Microsoft's own guidance is to design your system assuming prompt injection will happen.

System Prompt Leakage: Why Your "Secret Prompt" Isn't a Security Boundary ~ Davinder Tutorials

Documentation | OWASP - OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025.

docs.title: What is prompt injection?
docs.text:
Prompt injection is tricking the model into following an attacker's instructions instead of yours. OWASP has it at the top of the list as LLM01:2025.

There are two kinds:

  • Direct: the user types it in themselves. "Ignore previous instructions and..."
  • Indirect: the instructions are hidden in something the AI reads, like an email, a web page, a PDF, a ticket description, or white text on a white background. The user might have no idea. This is the scary one for agents, because an agent that reads a malicious email might then use its tools (send mail, run a query, change a setting) on the attacker's behalf.

The attack surface isn't only the model, it's the whole system built around it. Microsoft's defense-in-depth approach layers a few things because none of them are 100% on their own:

  • Prompt Shields in Microsoft Foundry scan prompts and documents for injection attempts.
  • Spotlighting marks outside content as untrusted so the model treats it as data, not instructions.
  • Least privilege and human approval on agent tools, so a successful injection can't do much.
  • Validating the model's output before your code acts on it.

For Microsoft 365 Copilot, jailbreak and injection detections show up as alerts in the Defender portal and Purview audit logs, which means you can hunt on them in Sentinel.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: What is ANI?
docs.text: Everything we actually have today, Claude, GPT, Copilot, every commercial AI tool, is Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI). These models are really good at the kinds of tasks they were trained for, but they don't learn on the job. Once training is done the weights are frozen, and anything "new" they know in a conversation is just whatever is sitting in the context window.

docs.title: What is AGI?
docs.text: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) would be human-level across the board: common sense, learning new things from a few examples, and handling any domain without being retrained for it. Nobody has built it, and there isn't even one agreed-on definition. Experts argue about whether it's years away, decades away, or the wrong goal entirely.

docs.title: Why does it matter?
docs.text: For my day to day it mostly doesn't. Don't let the AGI debate distract from what these tools can already do. There's a huge gap between "can do everything a human can" and "can draft my weekly Defender for Cloud summary so I just review it," and the second one is doable right now.

docs.title: What is the context window?
docs.text:
The context window is basically the LLM's working memory. It's the max number of tokens the model can look at in one request, and that includes everything: the system prompt, the conversation history, any documents you pasted in, tool results, and the answer the model writes back. Input and output share the same budget.

Something that surprised me: the model doesn't remember anything between requests. Every time you send a message, the app re-sends the whole conversation. The "memory" you see in a chat app is just the app stuffing the history back into the context window each time.

docs.title: What happens when you exceed it?
docs.text:
I used to think the model starts "replacing" old text on its own. That's not quite it. If you send a raw API request that's over the limit, it just fails. Azure OpenAI sends back a 400 error and the model never sees it.

The replacing happens in the app around the model (the harness). Chat apps and agent tools like Claude Code or the Azure OpenAI Assistants API trim older messages or summarize them to make room. So my database buffer pool comparison still works, just one layer up. The app is the buffer manager deciding what gets evicted, not the model.

Also, being under the limit doesn't mean the model pays equal attention to everything. Stuff buried in the middle of a really long context is more likely to get missed (researchers call it "lost in the middle"). A bigger context window doesn't automatically mean better answers.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn - How the Assistants API truncates to fit.

docs.title: Why does this matter when building AI tools?
docs.text:
• Agents pile up tokens on every loop, because each tool call result gets added to the context.
  • MCP tool definitions (the JSON that describes each tool) load into the context before you even ask anything. Connect a bunch of MCP servers and you've eaten space and money before any real work starts.
  • Big documents need to be chunked, summarized, or pulled in with RAG instead of pasted in whole.

Deciding what goes into the context window, when, and how much of it is called context engineering. It's a real skill, and it's most of what separates an agent that works from one that falls apart halfway through a task.

docs.title: How do diffusion models make images?
docs.text:
Image generation works totally differently from text generation. Most image models are diffusion models.

During training, the model takes a clean image and adds random static (Gaussian noise) step by step until the picture is unrecognizable. It learns how to undo each of those steps.

When you generate an image, it starts from pure noise and removes it a little at a time, using your prompt to steer what shows up. You're basically watching it pull a picture out of static.

Most modern models, like Stable Diffusion, don't do this on every pixel. They work on a compressed version of the image (latent space), which is a lot cheaper, and then decode it back into a full image at the end.

docs.title: Why does this matter for security?
docs.text: Deepfakes. The same tech makes it cheap to fake a face or a voice, and attackers are already using it for social engineering. In 2024 an employee at the engineering firm Arup was tricked into sending about $25 million after a video call where the "CFO" and other coworkers were all deepfakes. Out-of-band verification (calling back on a known number) matters more than ever.

docs.title: What is a large language model?
docs.text:
A large language model (LLM) is a deep learning model built on the transformer and trained on a massive amount of text to do one job: predict the next token. Given everything so far, what comes next? Get really good at that across trillions of tokens and the model picks up grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and code along the way.

That's why one LLM can summarize, classify sentiment, answer questions, translate, and write or explain code. It's not a different model for every task.

In the Microsoft world, Microsoft Security Copilot, Copilot Studio, and Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry all sit on top of LLMs. Knowing how the model works underneath explains a lot of why those tools act the way they do.

docs.title: How does a model go from nothing to useful?
docs.text:
1. Pre-training: the model reads internet-scale text and learns to predict the next token. What comes out is a foundation model (base model). It knows a lot, but it's not a helpful assistant yet. Ask a base model a question and it might just keep writing more questions. Think of it as a blank slab of marble.
  2. Post-training: this is what turns the base model into something you can actually talk to. It usually includes supervised fine-tuning (training on lots of example conversations with good answers) and reinforcement learning like RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), where people rate responses and the model gets rewarded for the ones they prefer. Labs also use AI feedback and automated checks now, not only humans.
  3. Your own fine-tuning (optional): companies can fine-tune a model even further on their own examples. I wrote about when that's worth it in RAG, CAG, and Memory.

docs.title: What does temperature actually change?
docs.text:
Every time the model picks the next token, it has a probability for every token in its vocabulary. Temperature changes how it picks from that list. It's basically how much risk you let the model take on its next word.

  • Low temperature (around 0 to 0.3) sticks to the most likely tokens. Answers are more focused and repeatable. This is what you want for KQL, code, or pulling facts out of a document.
  • High temperature (around 0.8 and up) gives the less likely tokens more of a chance. Answers get more creative and varied, and also more likely to go off the rails.

In Azure OpenAI, temperature goes from 0 to 2. Microsoft recommends changing either temperature or top_p (another sampling setting) but not both.

Two things that tripped me up:

  1. Temperature 0 doesn't make the model right, it makes it consistent. It can be consistently wrong.
  2. Most reasoning models, like the o-series in Azure OpenAI, don't support temperature at all. You tune them with reasoning_effort instead.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: What are reasoning models?
docs.text:
Regular LLMs start answering right away. Reasoning models spend extra compute "thinking" first. They generate a chain of thought (breaking the problem into steps, checking their work, backtracking when something doesn't add up) before giving the final answer. OpenAI's o-series, Claude with extended thinking, and DeepSeek R1 all work like this.

The trade-off is cost and time. Those thinking tokens get billed, so a reasoning model is overkill for "what's the KQL operator for contains?" but usually worth it for multi-step debugging or working through an incident timeline. In Azure OpenAI they also use max_completion_tokens instead of max_tokens.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: What is a neural network?
docs.text: A neural network is a bunch of connected nodes (neurons) stacked in layers. Data goes in one side, gets passed through the layers, and a prediction comes out the other side.

docs.title: How does a neural network learn?
docs.text:
Two things get adjusted while it learns: weights and biases.

Weights are like volume knobs on every connection between neurons. Turn one up and that connection matters more, turn it down and it matters less. Biases are extra numbers added at each neuron that shift the output, kind of like a starting baseline.

Learning happens in a loop:

  1. Forward pass: the input runs through the network and it makes a prediction.
  2. Loss: the prediction gets compared to the right answer. How far off it was is the loss (error).
  3. Backpropagation: the network works backward through the layers to figure out how much each weight contributed to that error.
  4. Gradient descent: every weight and bias gets nudged a tiny bit in whatever direction lowers the error.

That loop runs over and over on a huge amount of training data. Today's LLMs have billions of these weights, which is why you'll see them called "parameters" (like a 70B model = 70 billion parameters).

docs.title: What is a transformer and why did 2017 change everything?
docs.text:
Before 2017, language models mostly used recurrent neural networks (RNNs and LSTMs). They read a sentence one word at a time, in order. That's slow because you can't run it in parallel, and by the end of a long paragraph the model has kind of forgotten how it started.

In 2017 Google researchers published "Attention Is All You Need," which introduced the transformer. The main trick is self-attention: every token looks at every other token in the input at the same time and figures out which ones matter to it.

That's how a model knows "bank" means something different in "river bank" vs "bank account." And since it all happens at once instead of word by word, it runs really well on GPUs, which is a big reason models were able to get so large.

The original transformer had two halves. The encoder reads and understands the input, and the decoder generates the output. Most models today only use one half:

  • Encoder-only, like BERT. Good at understanding tasks like classification and search.
  • Decoder-only, like GPT, Claude, and Llama. Good at generating text, which is what every chatbot does.

Documentation | arXiv - The original "Attention Is All You Need" paper.

docs.title: What is Generative AI?
docs.text:
AI, machine learning, and deep learning get thrown around like they mean the same thing. They don't. The easiest way I think about it is circles inside circles.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the big circle. It's any system doing something that normally takes a human brain, and that includes old school rule-based systems where somebody hand wrote every "if this, then that."

Machine learning (ML) sits inside AI. Instead of a person writing the rules, the system learns the patterns from data.

Deep learning sits inside ML. It uses neural networks with a lot of layers, that's where the "deep" comes from.

Generative AI is the part of deep learning that creates new stuff (text, images, code, audio) instead of just labeling or predicting things. ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and image generators all live here.

So deep learning is ML and ML is AI, but it doesn't work the other way around. When a vendor says "we use AI" that could be a rules engine from the 90s or a model trained on half the internet, so it's worth asking which one.

docs.title: Subcategories
docs.text:
The nav is alphabetical, so here's the order I'd actually read them in:

  1. Neural Networks and Transformers
  2. Tokens and Embeddings
  3. Large Language Models
  4. Context Windows
  5. From Chatbots to Agents
  6. RAG, CAG, and Memory
  7. AI Flaws: Hallucinations and Prompt Injection
  8. Image Generation
  9. ANI vs AGI

docs.title: How it all connects
docs.text:
From the bottom up:

Deep learning (neural networks, weights, biases)
    ↓
Transformer (self-attention)
    ↓
Foundation model (pre-trained to predict the next token)
    ↓
Post-trained LLM (fine-tuning + RLHF so it acts like an assistant)
    ↓
Context window (everything the model can see in one request)
    ↓
Agent (LLM + tools + a loop)
    ↓
MCP and RAG (how the agent reaches tools and outside knowledge)
    ↓
Harness (everything around the model: rules, guardrails, permissions, orchestration)

Each layer sits on the one below it. If you understand how tokens, context windows, and prompt injection work, you'll make better calls building security tooling on top of AI than someone who's only following a tutorial.

docs.title: Why does a model need outside knowledge?
docs.text: An LLM only knows what it was trained on. That has a cutoff date and it definitely doesn't include your company's private docs. Prompting, RAG, CAG, and fine-tuning are all ways to get the model what it's missing.

docs.title: What's the difference between fine-tuning, RAG, and prompting, and when do you reach for each?
docs.text:
Microsoft's guidance is to start with prompting, add RAG when you need your own data, and only fine-tune after you've measured that the first two aren't cutting it. They aren't either/or, a lot of real apps use all three together.

Prompting: being specific in your request and giving the model the context, examples, and format you want back. This is always step one because it's free and you can change it in seconds. Reach for it when the model already knows enough and just needs direction, like "write a KQL query against SigninLogs that only returns failed sign-ins from the last 24 hours."

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): a separate library the model can look through. When you ask a question, the app searches your documents (company docs, runbooks, policies), grabs the most relevant chunks, and puts them in the context window next to your question. The model answers from those chunks. Reach for it when the answer depends on private or up-to-date data, or when you need to show where the answer came from. Example: an internal assistant that answers questions from your security policies and runbooks.

Fine-tuning: training a base model more on a set of example inputs and correct outputs so it learns a style, a format, or a narrow task. Reach for it when prompting can't get the behavior consistent (like always returning the same JSON structure), or when you want a smaller, cheaper model to do one specific job as well as a big one. Microsoft's example is fine-tuning a small model to turn plain English questions into SQL for their specific schema.

What I got wrong

I originally wrote that fine-tuning is "feeding all the data that matters to you." It can add domain knowledge, but for facts that change or need access controls, RAG is the better fit. Fine-tuned facts are baked in until you retrain, and the model can't tell you which document it got them from. Fine-tuning on bad data also makes the model worse, and a deployed fine-tuned model in Azure OpenAI charges hosting by the hour even when nobody is using it.

Fine-Tuning vs Prompting vs RAG: When to Use What - Beginners in AI

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: What's the security catch with RAG?
docs.text:
Two things:

  1. RAG has to respect permissions. If the search step pulls a document the user isn't allowed to see, the model will happily summarize it for them. The retrieval has to filter by the user's access before anything goes into the context window.
  2. Every document you retrieve is a way in for indirect prompt injection. If someone plants instructions in a doc your RAG pipeline reads, the model reads them too (more on that in AI Flaws).

docs.title: What is CAG?
docs.text: Cache-augmented generation (CAG) skips the search step. You load the whole knowledge base into the context window up front, and the provider caches it (prompt caching) so you're not paying full price or waiting on it every request. It's faster and simpler than RAG, but it only works when the data is small enough to fit and doesn't change much. RAG is still the default when you've got a lot of data.

docs.title: What are vector databases and grounding?
docs.text:
A vector database stores embeddings so you can search by meaning instead of by exact keywords. "Find me docs similar to this idea" instead of "find me docs containing these words." Azure AI Search, Cosmos DB, Azure SQL, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Pinecone, and Weaviate can all do this.

Grounding means tying the model's answer to real data you handed it, and RAG is the most common way to do it. Grounding cuts down on hallucinations but doesn't get rid of them, since the model can still misread or overstate what's in the doc.

docs.title: What is a token?
docs.text:
Tokens aren't letters, words, or phrases. They're the chunks a LLM breaks text into before it does anything with it. A token can be a whole word ("report"), part of a word ("ham" + "bur" + "ger"), a single character, or punctuation. For typical English text, one token is roughly 4 characters, or about ¾ of a word.

The chopping up is done by a tokenizer. GPT models use a method called Byte Pair Encoding (BPE). BPE starts with single characters and keeps merging the pairs that show up together the most until it has a vocabulary of common chunks. That's why common words are usually one token while rare words, code, and non-English text get split into more tokens (and cost more).

Every token gets a number (token ID). The model never actually sees your text, only those IDs.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: Why do tokens cost money?
docs.text:
It comes down to compute. Every token has to run through the model's billions of weights on a GPU, which is a ton of matrix math (multiplying giant grids of numbers). Output tokens are even more work because the model writes its answer one token at a time and runs the whole model again for each new one. On top of that, attention compares tokens to each other, so the longer your input is, the heavier every step gets.

That's why providers charge per token, usually listed per 1 million tokens, and output tokens usually cost more than input tokens. You pay both ways too. Send a 1,000 token prompt, get a 1,000 token answer back, and you're billed for about 2,000.

What I got wrong

I originally wrote that BPE was the GPU math that makes tokens expensive. BPE is just how the text gets split up, and that part is cheap. The expensive part is running the model on every single token.

AI Tokens Explained: What They Are and Why They Cost Money - Beginners in AI

Tech in Five - Tokens & Tokenomics - YouTube

Documentation | Microsoft Learn - How Azure OpenAI bills tokens.

docs.title: What is an embedding and how is it different from a token?
docs.text:
A token is basically a lookup number for a chunk of text. It doesn't say anything about meaning. An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents what the text means.

The numbers are laid out so similar meanings land close together in this huge multi-dimensional space. "Cat" and "dog" end up near each other, "laptop" ends up way over somewhere else. You can embed a single word, a sentence, or a whole chunk of a document.

The way I think about it: if a token is your employee ID number, an embedding is where your desk is in the office. People on the same team sit near each other.

To compare two embeddings you usually use cosine similarity, which measures the angle between the two vectors. Smaller angle means more similar meaning. That's what makes semantic search work, where "failed sign-in" can match a doc that says "authentication error" even though none of the words are the same.

This matters for security in two ways:

  • Embeddings power vector search and RAG. Azure AI Search, Cosmos DB, Azure SQL, and PostgreSQL (pgvector) can all store and search them.
  • Embeddings of sensitive documents are still sensitive data. OWASP calls this out as LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, so lock down your vector store like any other database.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: 1. Describe how you would design a secure, multi-account AWS and Azure environment for a SaaS company handling sensitive enterprise data.
docs.text:
1. Limit the blast radius and set up a hierarchy. AWS has Organizations, which lets you create Organizational Units (OUs) based on the environment (like a Security OU), and under that OU you create separate accounts for each job (like a Log Archive account, Security Tooling account, Network account, etc.).

    Azure has Management Groups and Subscriptions. You can make management groups for Production, Non-Production, and so on, then isolate dev and test environments at the subscription level.

  2. Identity and access management. Attackers don't have to work that hard exploiting vulnerabilities anymore when they can just scan the internet for leaked access keys and credentials. Having a single source of truth for identity helps a lot. I'm biased, so I'd say Entra ID should be your IdP and you federate AWS to it. In Entra ID you can use Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for just-in-time access to highly privileged roles that need approval. On the AWS side, IAM Identity Center hands out short-lived credentials through roles, so people don't need long-term IAM user access keys at all.

  3. Network security and isolation. Segment your network with VNets (Azure) and VPCs (AWS), then use private endpoints. You don't want your database taking requests from the internet. Firewalls are also a great tool here, since they inspect traffic going in and out of your environment.

  4. Data protection: at rest, in transit, and in use. Use customer-managed keys (CMKs) in AWS KMS and Azure Key Vault. That gives your company control over key rotation and revocation. And please never hard-code secrets... it wouldn't be a secret if you did. AWS Secrets Manager and Azure Key Vault exist so you can pull and rotate database credentials, API keys, and a lot more through code. You also need to know what data your company has and where it lives. May I suggest Microsoft Purview...

  5. All of this sounds good, but without the right governance you won't get far, lol. You need a way to manage the complexity of multicloud, centralized visibility, and automated compliance. That means cloud security posture management (CSPM) like Defender for Cloud, AWS SCPs for hard guardrails (like stopping anyone from turning off logging, or only allowing resources in certain regions), and Azure Policy.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Organized and created OUs:

    • Infrastructure (shared services and network resources)
    • Workloads (application environments)
    • Exceptions (temporary policy exemptions)
    • Sandbox (developer experimentation)
    • Onboarding (mergers and acquisitions)
    • Nursery (new accounts before they get deployed)
    • Suspended (accounts marked for deprovisioning)
    • IncidentResponse (accounts with an active security incident)

    Chris Farris GitHub repo that deploys OUs with Terraform

  2. Created two new AWS accounts and moved them to the Security OU:

    • IAM (just for identity and access management)
    • SecurityOperations (holds security tools that can make changes)

    Why?

    • Keeping IAM in its own account isolates identity management, which cuts down on privilege escalation risk.
    • The SecurityOperations account gives security tools a controlled place to live.

docs.title: But Why?
docs.text:
1. Why separate OUs? To organize accounts by their security and operational needs.
  2. Why does organization matter? It makes it a lot easier to enforce access control and security policies.
  3. Why enforce strict access control? To limit the blast radius of a breach.
  4. Why minimize the blast radius? So a compromised account or a misconfiguration does less damage.
  5. Why care about misconfigurations? They're one of the top causes of cloud security incidents.

docs.title: Another Me SSO with IAM Identity Center, Part 2
The Lesson
docs.text:
• Permissions get handed out with something called a permission set. A permission set can have up to 10 AWS managed or customer managed policies (you can raise that to 20 with a quota increase) plus one inline policy.
  • To give someone access to an account, you assign a user or group a permission set and the accounts. It's a 3 part equation: group + permission set + account = what you can do.
  • Users and groups can have multiple permission sets per account.
  • When you assign a permission set, Identity Center creates an IAM role in the account with the policies you picked. Then it sets the role's trust policy so the identity provider (IAM Identity Center) can assume it.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Created an AdministratorAccess permission set.

    Relay state is just a fancy way of saying "when the user logs in with this permission set, drop them in this part of the console."

  2. Gave the group AdministratorAccess to the SecurityAudit and management accounts.

    You have to select the accounts first, then click 'Assign users or groups'.

  3. Looked at the AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess role.

  1. This is the ARN of the identity provider that Identity Center/Organizations created in the account. You can see it under Identity providers. An AWS account can have more than one of these.
  2. This gives the role permission to use the AssumeRoleWithSAML API call, which is a little different from AssumeRole but really similar.
  3. This lets the IdP tag the session when you assume the role. That's really useful for tracking, because it adds a session name that matches the user who assumed the role.
  4. The last part is a condition that ONLY allows this when you come through the sign-in portal, and ONLY the AWS one. You can't assume this role from anywhere else.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Assumed the OrganizationAccountAccessRole.

    You have to put in the account ID of the account you want to switch into (SecurityAudit) and the role name (OrganizationAccountAccessRole).

  2. Deployed an S3 bucket in the SecurityAudit account for centralized logging.

    Centralizing logs is a big part of any cloud security strategy. With all the logs in one place, the security team can investigate and watch for suspicious activity across every account without hopping around.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• AWS doesn't let you assume roles with the root user. You have to use an IAM user or another role.
  • AWS Security Token Service (STS) is the service that hands out temporary, limited-privilege credentials when you assume a role.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• IAM Identity Center lets you manage user access centrally, so you don't have to create separate IAM users in every AWS account.
  • Federation lets one identity source (like Microsoft Entra ID or Okta) manage access across a bunch of AWS accounts and services.
  • Identity Provider (IdP): where you log in. The IdP is home to the user pool or directory where you set up user accounts, groups, etc. We sometimes call it the authoritative source because it's the final word on who you are and what groups and roles you have.
  • Relying Party: where you do things. The relying party... relies... on the IdP for authentication, so it can focus on authorization.
  • Users get created in the IdP and assigned attributes like group, role, and email address.
  • Admins set up a trust relationship between the IdP and the relying party. This is usually an exchange of metadata that defines the relationship, the signing certificate(s), and the URLs they use to talk to each other.
  • A user logs into the IdP. When they go to log into a relying party, they provide the IdP's address or some other identifier so the relying party knows where to send them (this is usually hidden from the user).
  • The IdP then makes an assertion: a digitally signed statement that the user is who they say they are, plus whatever attributes it sends over (like a group, or whether they used MFA).
  • The user gets a token that represents the session. That token has a Time To Live (TTL) before it expires. The user just shows the token to the relying party, and the relying party decides what they're allowed to do.
  • When the token expires, the user has to log in again or get a refreshed token with a new TTL.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Deployed AWS IAM Identity Center (it used to be called AWS SSO).
  2. Turned on MFA for every sign-in under settings.
  3. Created a user and an Administrator group, and added the user to the group.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Updated the alternate contacts (billing, security, operations) for the management account.
  2. Created a Prod and a NonProd account under the Workloads OU.

Org Kickstart

docs.title: Create Your First AWS IAM Role
The Lesson
docs.text:
• IAM roles are how you manage permissions for services and users in AWS. Roles are more secure than users because they use temporary credentials.
  • A persona is how an identity shows up in a certain context. It's basically a role a user can assume to get a temporary set of permissions for a session.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Created a new IAM role for EC2 instances to assume so they can talk to SSM (Systems Manager).

    The trusted entity is who's allowed to assume the role.

    The permissions policies define what the role can do. Here it lets the EC2 instance run SSM commands for system management and not much else, which is least privilege.

    Why it matters: using an IAM role for EC2 to work with Systems Manager means you don't need SSH keys or long-lived API credentials, which are dangerous if they get leaked.

docs.title: Create and Secure Your First Admin User
The Lab
docs.text:
1. Logged into AWS using the root account.

    The root account has unrestricted access to everything in the account, which makes it a big target. Only use it when you have to and always protect it with MFA. We only needed it here for the first setup before switching to a lower-privilege account. AWS actually requires MFA on root users now.

  2. Created an IAM group ("Administrators").

    IAM groups let you manage permissions in one place. Attaching policies to a group instead of to each user keeps permissions consistent and a lot easier to manage as more people get added.

  3. Created an IAM user and added it to the Administrators group.

    Using an IAM user instead of root means admin actions can be logged, audited, and revoked if needed. Getting permissions through the group keeps things consistent so you don't end up with one-off misconfigurations.

  4. Turned on MFA for the IAM user.

    MFA adds another factor on top of the password, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in.

What AWS recommends now

This lab uses an IAM user to get started, but AWS's current guidance is that people (human users) should sign in through federation with IAM Identity Center and get temporary credentials, not long-term IAM users. The later SSO labs switch over to that.

docs.title: Why is IAM Important?
docs.text:
• IAM controls access to every cloud resource. Every request, from a person or a machine, has to go through IAM.
  • Since AWS is reachable from the internet, IAM is the first and most important security layer you have.
  • The biggest cloud breaches usually come from misconfigured IAM policies, exposed credentials, or way too much access.
  • You'll hear "identity is the new perimeter" a lot. In traditional networks, firewalls and VPNs were the perimeter. In the cloud, it's IAM.

docs.title: Main Concepts in IAM
docs.text:
1. Entity: a person, device, or system that needs access to AWS.
  2. Identity: a unique representation of an entity (like an IAM user, role, or federated identity).
  3. Identifier: a way to prove an identity, usually tied to credentials or cryptographic tokens.

AWS IAM is built around identities and policies:

  • The root user is tied to an email address and has unrestricted control.
  • IAM users live inside an AWS account and have less privilege than root.
  • IAM roles and policies define who can access what, and how.

docs.title: Bonus
docs.text: ARNs (Amazon Resource Names) uniquely identify resources across AWS, so a new resource that reuses an old name doesn't accidentally inherit someone's old permissions. Understanding ARNs helps a lot with writing permissions, reading logs, and securing resources.

docs.title: Creating Security Team Permissions in IAM Identity Center
The Lesson
docs.text: • So nobody is running around with full admin all the time, give out different permission sets (read-only, full admin, IAM admin) in IAM Identity Center based on the task. That limits the damage from an accident or a compromised account.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Assigned the AdministratorAccess permission set to the Admin group for the IAM, SecurityAudit, SecurityOperations, and TestAccount1 accounts.

    This is there for incident responders in case they need to "break glass" and jump into an account that's under active attack.

  2. Created more groups: SecurityAdministrators and IAM Administrators.

  3. Created more permission sets: ReadOnly and IdentityCenterAdministrator.

    IdentityCenterAdministrator uses the AWS managed policy AWSSSOMemberAccountAdministrator.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Turned on AWS Organizations.

    Organizations lets you manage a bunch of AWS accounts from one place, which is a best practice once you have more than one account. It gives you a clean way to split things up by business unit, environment, or security boundary.

  2. Created an OU (Organizational Unit) named 'Security' and moved the 'LogArchive' account into it.

    OUs are containers for AWS accounts, so you can group accounts by business or security needs.

    OUs also let you apply Service Control Policies (SCPs), which control what's allowed in every account under that OU.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• OrganizationAccountAccessRole lets the management account get into the new account as an administrator. It gets created automatically when you create an account from Organizations, and it means you don't have to manage separate IAM users in every account. In other words, the role trusts the whole management account, so anyone in the management account with permission to assume roles can use it.
  • Service Control Policies (SCPs) restrict what actions are allowed in each account, which protects your sensitive resources.
  • The account you turn Organizations on in becomes your management account. DO NOT DEPLOY WORKLOADS IN THAT ACCOUNT.
  • With consolidated billing, member accounts roll their charges up to the management account but are otherwise still independent.

docs.title: Enabled Delegated Administrator for Identity Center and CloudTrail
The Lesson
docs.text:
• Delegated administration lets you hand control of certain AWS services to other accounts. That keeps people out of the management account and spreads out admin responsibilities, which is least privilege at the account level.

    The management account has huge power over every account in the organization. A lot of AWS services need the management account to get set up, so people end up using it all the time. If it gets compromised, an attacker basically owns everything.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Delegated IAM Identity Center to the IAM account in the Security OU.

    Identity Center handles authentication and authorization for everyone, so it's a big deal. Delegating it means day-to-day admin work doesn't need the management account.

  2. Delegated CloudTrail to the SecurityAudit account.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• GuardDuty is basically an IDS (intrusion detection system) for AWS. It looks at a bunch of telemetry sources to find possible threats.
  • GuardDuty charges based on how much data it analyzes, so it's cheap to turn on in every region, even ones you don't use.
  • Out of the box it watches CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs. You don't have to turn those logs on yourself. There are also extra protection plans (S3, EKS, Runtime Monitoring, Malware Protection, RDS, Lambda) you can add.
  • A lot of security frameworks require continuous threat monitoring, and GuardDuty is the AWS-native way to check that box.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Turned on GuardDuty in the primary region (us-east-1).

    GuardDuty is a regional service, so you have to turn it on separately in every region you care about.

  2. Did the same in the secondary region (us-west-2).

    Best practice is to turn GuardDuty on in every region, even ones you don't use. It costs almost nothing in a region with no activity (and our SCP blocks people from deploying there anyway).

    We also delegated GuardDuty administration to the SecurityAudit account.

  3. Set GuardDuty to auto-enable for accounts in the organization.

    In the delegated admin account you choose New (only accounts that join from now on), All (every account, including the ones already in the org), or None. If you pick New, you still have to add your existing accounts as members yourself.

docs.title: Enabling the Org Trail (Centralized Logging Part 3)
The Lab
docs.text:
1. Turned on trusted access for CloudTrail in Organizations.

  2. Turned on logging for all accounts in the organization.

    Switched roles into the SecurityAudit account, went into the trail we already made, and pointed it at the bucket we made earlier as the central logging location.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• Surprise charges are often a sign of an attack or a misconfiguration. Billing alerts are an extra layer of detection that can catch cryptomining, denial of service attacks, or resources someone forgot about.
  • CloudWatch lets you watch resource usage, performance, and billing metrics in one place, so you can catch problems early and avoid surprise bills.
  • SNS is a big part of security alerting. Sending alerts to admins by email (or other ways) means the team actually finds out about security incidents or weird billing.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Signed into root to turn on IAM access to billing information.

    By default, IAM users can't see billing data. Letting your non-root admin see it means the people watching security can spot unexpected charges and act fast.

  2. Turned on CloudWatch billing alerts.

    CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring service and it can track a lot of metrics, including billing. Once billing alerts are on, you can set alarms for specific spending thresholds. (Billing metrics only live in us-east-1.)

  3. Created a billing alarm with a $25 threshold.

    This is your safety net for unexpected charges. Cryptomining or a misconfigured resource can run up a huge bill, and the alarm tells you before it gets out of control.

  4. Connected the alarm to an SNS topic.

    Linking the alarm to SNS is what actually sends you an email (or another notification) when the threshold gets crossed.

  5. Subscribed to the SNS topic.

    The last step, so the notification actually reaches you. Getting told right away is what lets you stop a cryptomining attack or fix a misconfigured service before it costs you more.

Tip

AWS Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection are worth turning on too. Budgets can alert on forecasted spend, and Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to flag spending that doesn't match your normal pattern.

docs.title: Give Your Account a Security Blanket with SCPs
The Lab
docs.text:
1. Turned on Service Control Policies (SCPs).

    This attaches an allow-all SCP called FullAWSAccess to every OU and account. It basically says "nothing is blocked at the org level."

    Even with FullAWSAccess in place, users still need IAM permissions to actually use any services. The SCP doesn't give anyone access, it just doesn't take any away.

  2. Made a custom SCP to protect the root user and stop accounts from leaving the organization.

    ProtectRootAndOrg denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action and blocks the root user from doing anything.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Action": [
        "organizations:LeaveOrganization"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Effect": "Deny"
    },
    {
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:root"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

  1. Applied the SCP at the 'Root' level.

    Now no account can remove itself from the organization or use its root user.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• SCPs set the boundaries for what can happen in an account. They're like a filter on top of IAM policies at the organization level. SCPs never grant permissions by themselves. They set the maximum, and IAM policies still have to allow the action.
  • In AWS, an explicit deny always wins over an allow, no matter where the allow comes from.
  • SCPs don't apply to the management account, which is one more reason not to run anything in it.
  • AWS also has centralized root access management now. From the management account (or a delegated admin), you can remove the root credentials from member accounts completely and do the few root-only tasks with short-term root sessions instead.

docs.title: NotWhat?!? Lock Out Regions with a Double Negative SCP
The Lesson
docs.text:
• AWS has a lot of regions to help with regulatory compliance, disaster recovery, and performance.
  • Security settings have to be set up per region, and developers might deploy stuff in a region that doesn't have your security controls without realizing it.
  • Attackers love under-protected regions for things like cryptomining, since nobody's watching them.
  • Every region AWS launched before March 2019 is turned on by default in every account, and you can't turn those off. Newer regions are opt-in. Either way, an SCP is how you actually block the regions you don't use.
  • We use double negatives in AWS policies because they let us say "block everything except this." That keeps us safe even when AWS adds new services, actions, or regions.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Attached the RegionLockout SCP at the root level.
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "DenyAllOutsideRegions",
            "Effect": "Deny",
            "NotAction": [
                "a4b:*",
                "acm:*",
                "aws-marketplace-management:*",
                "aws-marketplace:*",
                "aws-portal:*",
                "budgets:*",
                "ce:*",
                "chime:*",
                "cloudfront:*",
                "config:*",
                "cur:*",
                "directconnect:*",
                "ec2:DescribeRegions",
                "ec2:DescribeTransitGateways",
                "ec2:DescribeVpnGateways",
                "fms:*",
                "globalaccelerator:*",
                "health:*",
                "iam:*",
                "importexport:*",
                "kms:*",
                "mobileanalytics:*",
                "networkmanager:*",
                "organizations:*",
                "pricing:*",
                "route53:*",
                "route53domains:*",
                "route53-recovery-cluster:*",
                "route53-recovery-control-config:*",
                "route53-recovery-readiness:*",
                "s3:GetAccountPublic*",
                "s3:ListAllMyBuckets",
                "s3:ListMultiRegionAccessPoints",
                "s3:PutAccountPublic*",
                "shield:*",
                "sts:*",
                "support:*",
                "trustedadvisor:*",
                "waf-regional:*",
                "waf:*",
                "wafv2:*",
                "wellarchitected:*"
            ],
            "Resource": "*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringNotEquals": {
                    "aws:RequestedRegion": [
                        "us-east-1",
                        "us-west-2"
                    ]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

  • The NotAction denies everything except the actions in that list. Those are global services, and if you block them everything breaks. Documentation | AWS. But why? Instead of denying thousands of actions one by one, we list the small set of actions to let through.

  • The condition means: if an API call is NOT going to one of these two regions, block it.

  • Before deploying this SCP, check which regions you actually use with the Billing console and IAM Access Advisor. Test it on a test OU before rolling it out everywhere.

docs.title: OUs, SCPs, and a Root User Account Recovery
The Lesson
docs.text:
1. Why move the SCP off the root?
    • So we can have an Exceptions OU that's allowed to use root temporarily.
  2. Why do we need an Exceptions OU?
    • Some admin tasks, like changing the root email, need the root user.
  3. Why can't we just change the root user directly?
    • The ProtectRootAndOrg SCP blocks root actions, so those changes would get denied.
  4. Why does this matter for security?
    • Controlled, temporary exceptions keep governance in place while still letting you do the admin tasks you have to do.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Attached the ProtectRootAndOrg SCP to every OU except the Exceptions OU.

  2. Detached the same SCP from Root.

    If we left it on Root, it would still apply to Exceptions because SCPs inherit down.

  3. Moved the SecurityAudit account into the Exceptions OU so I could change its root email and rename it to LogArchive.

    "Securely" recovered the root user for SecurityAudit.

  4. Moved LogArchive back into the Security OU and created a new SecurityAudit account in the same OU.

Note

AWS has centralized root access management now. Instead of the Exceptions OU dance, the management account (or a delegated admin) can remove root credentials from member accounts and run root-only tasks with short-term root sessions.

docs.title: On the Meaning of Life(cycles), Versions, and Ransomware
The Lesson
docs.text:
• Keeping every log forever can turn into a big bill, even if it starts small.
  • Security logs should be managed on purpose. Retention should balance what compliance needs with what storage costs.
  • A lifecycle policy decides what to keep, what to move to cheaper storage, and what to delete.
  • S3 versioning keeps previous versions of objects, which makes it a lot harder for an attacker to permanently delete data. Attackers delete or change logs to cover their tracks.
  • You can block delete operations on critical logs with IAM policies or an SCP.
  • Why didn't we use versioning in this lab? It increases storage costs. For real ransomware protection though, versioning + SCPs are highly recommended. S3 Object Lock is the feature that actually makes objects immutable (write once, read many).
  • S3 Glacier storage classes are cheap for long-term storage, but some of them are slow to get data back from. Glacier Flexible Retrieval can take minutes to hours, and Glacier Deep Archive can take 12 hours or more. During an investigation you need logs fast, so that wait might not work. (Glacier Instant Retrieval is the exception, it's milliseconds.)

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Signed into LogArchive with the AdministratorAccess role through SSO and turned on an S3 lifecycle policy for the CloudTrail bucket for 90 days.

    90 days of retention keeps logs around for incident response and audits.

docs.title: PBAC and ABAC Write an Intermediate AWS IAM Policy
The Lesson
docs.text:
• Access controls map to objects (like files or systems), authorizations map to actions (like AWS API calls), and entitlements are when you assign either one to an identity.
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): assigns roles to identities, and the roles define the permissions.
  • Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC): uses attributes like tags and IP addresses to decide access.
  • Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC): writes both RBAC and ABAC rules into policies.
  • Statements: define the permissions (Effect: allow or deny the actions).
  • Actions: the specific API operations being allowed or denied.
  • Resources: the AWS resources the policy applies to.
  • Conditions: extra rules based on attributes.
  • Conditions in IAM policies have two main parts:
    1. Condition keys, which either apply to everything (like aws:SourceIp) or to a specific service (like s3:ResourceTag). Documentation | AWS
    2. Condition operators, which are the logic like StringEquals, IpAddress, and Bool. Documentation | AWS

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text: 1. Wrote (and then deleted) an IAM policy that lets you stop or start an instance only when the API call comes from a certain IP address.

docs.title: Secure that Bucket! (Centralized Logging Part 2), Resource Policies
The Lesson
docs.text:
• Resource-based policies (like bucket policies) are attached to the resource itself instead of to an identity. You need them when something outside your account (another account, an AWS service, or even the public internet) has to reach the resource, so getting them right is a big deal.
  • Adding conditions like aws:SourceArn and s3:x-amz-acl makes sure only the service or user you intended can touch your resource. That helps stop things like data exfiltration or another account's trail writing into your bucket.
  • A deny always overrides an allow, so you can use deny statements to block actions even if some other policy allows them.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Customized the given bucket policy and applied it to the logging bucket.
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "AWSCloudTrailAclCheck20150319",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": {
                "Service": [
                    "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
                ]
            },
            "Action": "s3:GetBucketAcl",
            "Resource": "<Bucket ARN>",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:SourceArn": "<Trail ARN>"
                }
            }
        },
        {
            "Sid": "AWSCloudTrailWrite20150319",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": {
                "Service": [
                    "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
                ]
            },
            "Action": "s3:PutObject",
            "Resource": "<Bucket ARN>/AWSLogs/<Management AccountID>/*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "s3:x-amz-acl": "bucket-owner-full-control",
                    "aws:SourceArn": "<Trail ARN>"
                }
            }
        },
        {
            "Sid": "AWSCloudTrailOrganizationWrite20150319",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": {
                "Service": [
                    "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
                ]
            },
            "Action": "s3:PutObject",
            "Resource": "<Bucket ARN>/AWSLogs/<organizationID>/*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "s3:x-amz-acl": "bucket-owner-full-control",
                    "aws:SourceArn": "<Trail ARN>"
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

The first statement lets the CloudTrail service read the bucket's access control list (ACL), but only when the request comes from the trail in the management account.

The second statement lets CloudTrail write objects into the bucket under the /AWSLogs/<Management AccountID>/ path, but only if the write sets bucket-owner-full-control and comes from the management account's trail.

The last statement lets CloudTrail write into the same bucket, but under the organization ID path, which is where the org trail puts logs for every account.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Made a customer managed policy.

    The policy lets the IAM admins create, list, get, update, and delete IAM policies.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
I got a 404 status error: Not supported policy message when I tried to attach the ManagePoliciesForIdentityCenter policy to the IAM permission set. I Googled it and found this solution. It looked like I had to create the same policy in the IAM account before it could attach to the permission set.

Then I saw why I got the error... I was creating and adding the permission set in my management account instead of my IAM account with the admin access role. Customer managed policies in a permission set have to exist (with the same name) in every account you assign the permission set to.

docs.title: The Best Way to Start with AWS Security Hub
docs.text:
Security Hub changed

At the end of 2025, AWS launched a new, unified AWS Security Hub that correlates signals from GuardDuty, Inspector, and CSPM checks and adds exposure findings and attack path visualization. The original Security Hub I used in this lab (security standards and controls) is now called AWS Security Hub CSPM. The lessons below still apply, the names just moved around.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• Security Hub collects findings from almost every other AWS security service in one place and normalizes them into a standard format.
  • Security Hub (now Security Hub CSPM) works as a cloud security posture management (CSPM) tool. Think of CSPM as a vulnerability scanner for your cloud configuration. It checks how you have things set up, like your S3 buckets, and flags problems like a public bucket.
  • In Security Hub, the sets of rules it checks are called security standards.
  • CloudTrail tells us most of what's going on in our account (at least the API calls), and GuardDuty uses threat detection to find possibly malicious activity like cryptomining and brute force attacks.
  • Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions.
  • The security standards use AWS Config behind the scenes, and Config can get expensive.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Turned on Security Hub in us-east-1.

    Disabled the security standards (they were on by default).

    Delegated Security Hub administration to the SecurityAudit account.

    Turned on Security Hub only for findings aggregation, not the full security scanning.

  2. Configured Security Hub in the SecurityAudit account.

    Checked and disabled the security standards again.

    Started central configuration and made sure the home region stayed N. Virginia (us-east-1).

    Picked "Customize my Security Hub configuration" so AWS didn't automatically turn on extra security features.

    Disabled the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard to keep costs low.

docs.title: Questions I Ask Myself
docs.text:
1. Why do we always have to turn on security services in the management account? In this lab, we signed into the management account, turned on Security Hub, and delegated it to SecurityAudit. Why couldn't we just turn it on in SecurityAudit?

    If you turn a security service on in the SecurityAudit account by itself, it only covers that one account. Turning it on from the management account (and delegating from there) is what sets it up to cover every account in the organization.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text: • CloudFormation lets you define infrastructure in declarative templates (infrastructure as code, IaC). IaC makes things consistent and repeatable, so there's less chance of a manual mistake turning into a security problem (like a misconfigured permission or exposed data).

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
• Pasted a template URL to create an SNS topic and named it "SecurityAlerts". Did this in us-east-1.

    Deploying SNS topics with IaC means your security alert notifications get set up the same way every time, so you can respond quickly when something happens.

    Always check where an IaC template came from and what's in it before you deploy it. Regular reviews and automated security checks (like scanning for hardcoded credentials) should be part of the process.

AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Template to create a SNS topic named SecurityAlerts
Resources:
  SecurityAlertsTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      TopicName: SecurityAlerts

The Resources block has everything you want it to build. Type is what we're building, and Properties are the configuration settings.

  • To get alerts we subscribe to a topic. Subscriptions can be text messages, emails, or fancier internal stuff for building event-driven notification systems for apps.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• CloudTrail is a central record of almost every admin action (API call) in an AWS account.
  • Turn on multi-region trails so you're logging everywhere, not just one region.
  • Store the logs in a private, encrypted S3 bucket. CloudTrail encrypts logs with SSE-S3 by default, and you can use your own KMS key (SSE-KMS) for more control over who can decrypt them.
  • In this lab we skipped the custom KMS key to keep it simple, since it's one more thing to manage. In a real environment, SSE-KMS is worth it for your security logs.
  • Make sure log file validation is on. It uses hashing and digital signatures so you can prove the logs weren't changed or deleted, which matters for forensics.
  • Management events: admin actions (like IAM changes or EC2 changes).
  • Data events: access to the resources themselves (like S3 object reads/writes). These cost extra.
  • Insights events: flags unusual API activity. These cost extra too.

docs.title: Use EventBridge for Security Hub Alerts
The Lesson
docs.text:
• In cloud security, real-time events tell you what's happening right now, which is different from log files that take time to process.
  • Logs look backward. They have to be collected, stored, and analyzed, and all that adds delay before you detect anything. Events let you respond right away, so there's less time between detection and action.
  • Attackers take advantage of gaps when alerts are slow. Using events lets the security team act in near real time and stop or limit a threat before it does damage.
  • Why can't we just process logs faster? Storing and analyzing logs takes a lot of infrastructure and compute, so there's always some delay.
  • What is EventBridge? A service that lets AWS resources react to event patterns in real time.
  • Why is it useful? Security Hub findings, GuardDuty findings, and CloudTrail API activity all show up as events, and you can act on them right away by routing them through EventBridge.
  • Events are like salmon jumping out of a river: if you don't catch them when they show up, they're gone (ephemeral).

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Deployed an SNS topic that notifies us by email.

    Don't forget to subscribe to the topic.

  2. Created an EventBridge rule.

    Whenever a new finding gets imported into Security Hub, an alert goes off.

docs.title: The Lesson
docs.text:
• The ARN uniquely identifies an AWS resource, so you can point at exactly the right thing in an IAM policy. Getting the resource scope right means access only goes to what it should (like just the logs in this case) and nothing else gets exposed.
  • Inline policies attach directly to a user, group, or role and only work for the thing they're attached to. You write them for that one identity and can't reuse them anywhere else.
  • Managed policies are central policies you write once and attach wherever you want. If you update a managed policy, the change applies right away to everything using it. There are two kinds:
    • AWS managed policies are the standard ones AWS writes and maintains for customers to use.
    • Customer managed policies are ones you write yourself, and they only exist in your AWS account.

docs.title: The Lab
docs.text:
1. Created a custom policy for read (s3:GetObject) and write (s3:PutObject) on our CloudTrail bucket.

    IAM policies define what actions users, roles, and services can do, and writing your own gives you granular control. The visual policy editor makes it easier to build one if you're not comfortable with JSON yet.

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:GetObject",
                "s3:PutObject"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::rmogull-slaw/*"
        }
    ]
}

  • Version: the policy language version. "2012-10-17" is the current one and you should always include it.

  • Statement: the main part of the policy. It's an array of statements (anything in [] is an array). Each statement needs an effect, an action, and a resource.

  • Effect: whether the statement allows or denies.

  • Action: the specific actions (API calls) being allowed or denied. In this policy:

    • "s3:GetObject": lets you download objects from the bucket.
    • "s3:PutObject": lets you upload or overwrite objects in the bucket.

  • Resource: what the statement applies to.

    • Here, "arn:aws:s3:::rmogull-slaw/*" means the policy applies to all objects (/*) in the rmogull-slaw bucket.
    • An ARN (Amazon Resource Name) uniquely identifies an AWS resource. In this case it's my S3 bucket.

docs.title: Managing Security Operations in Microsoft Azure
docs.text:
Name changes

These are practice questions from an older course. Azure Security Center is Microsoft Defender for Cloud now, and Azure Active Directory is Microsoft Entra ID. I left the old names in the questions but updated the answers.

  1. What does the Azure Security Center investigation graph cover?

    A specific entity and the entities that are related to it.

  2. In the Azure portal, you configure App Service authentication so all anonymous requests to /.auth/login/<provider> get redirected to the chosen provider. You get an anonymous request from a native mobile app. What response does the mobile app most likely get back?

    HTTP 401 Unauthorized. Browsers get redirected to the sign-in page (HTTP 302), but native mobile apps get a 401. I originally had HTTP 200 OK here, which is wrong.

  3. Which feature encrypts data both at rest and in motion in an Azure SQL database?

    Always Encrypted. The data gets encrypted on the client side, so it stays encrypted in the database and on the way there, and even the DB admins can't read it.

  4. When should you run a security playbook in Security Center?

    When you need to respond to a specific security alert. In Defender for Cloud this is called workflow automation, and it runs a Logic App.

  5. Which operating systems are supported by the Microsoft Monitoring Agent?

    Windows and Linux VMs. The Microsoft Monitoring Agent (Log Analytics agent) was retired in August 2024 though, so use the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) now. It also supports Windows and Linux.

  6. In a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) model, which responsibility moves to Microsoft?

    Applying security patches to the operating system.

  7. You want to connect a Windows VM to a Linux VM. Which protocol should you use and what kind of key?

    Secure Shell (SSH) and SSH keys.

  8. What Azure service can you use for inbound protection at the perimeter?

    Azure Application Gateway (with its Web Application Firewall turned on).

  9. What's the name of Azure's load balancer service that includes a web application firewall and protects HTTP traffic?

    Azure Application Gateway

  10. You're reviewing Security Center recommendations and there's a vulnerability in a network security group. Which category is it?

    High severity

  11. What protocol does Azure Active Directory use to authorize access to web apps and web APIs?

    OAuth 2.0

docs.title: Microsoft Defender Suite
docs.text:
• Microsoft Defender for Cloud

    • Has policy and compliance metrics, a secure score to push you toward good security hygiene, and alerts for resources that aren't secure.

    • Secure score is a percentage based KPI that tells you how good (or bad) your security posture is.

    • Cloud security posture management (CSPM) is how you find and fix misconfigurations and compliance violations across a multicloud environment (Azure, AWS, GCP) before someone takes advantage of them.

    • The Defender plans (Defender for Servers, Storage, SQL, Containers, and more) add threat protection for specific workloads on top of the posture stuff.

  • Microsoft Defender for Identity

    • Watches your users (their activity and info) and builds a baseline of normal behavior, so it can flag things that don't fit.

    • It maps what it sees to the stages of an attack (the cyber kill chain), like recon, lateral movement, and domain dominance.

    • It uses signals from your on-premises Active Directory to find advanced threats, compromised identities, and malicious insiders.

    • It also covers AD FS, AD CS, and Entra Connect servers, so your whole hybrid identity setup is watched and not just the domain controllers.

  • Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

    • Helps you prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to threats on devices across your organization, before and after a breach.

    • Vulnerability management: finds, prioritizes, and helps you fix vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on your endpoints. This is called Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management now.

    • Attack surface reduction: makes devices harder to attack with things like ASR rules, application control, network protection, and web protection.

    • Next-generation protection: the antivirus part. It uses behavior-based and cloud-delivered protection to catch new threats.

    • Endpoint detection and response (EDR): catches the advanced stuff that got past the earlier layers. This is also where advanced hunting (KQL against device data) and custom detections come in.

    • Automated investigation and remediation: investigates alerts and fixes issues automatically so the SOC isn't doing everything by hand.

    • Microsoft Defender Experts: Microsoft's own analysts doing managed hunting and response for you. This used to be called Microsoft Threat Experts.

    • Management and APIs: you can manage it with Intune, Group Policy, or third party tools, and its API lets you automate workflows. It plugs into Microsoft Sentinel, Defender for Cloud, and the rest of the Defender stack.

  • Microsoft Defender XDR (used to be called Microsoft 365 Defender)

    • Pulls signals from all the Defender products (Endpoint, Identity, Office 365, Cloud Apps) and correlates them into one incident that tells the story of the attack. So a weird process on a laptop from Defender for Endpoint and a suspicious sign-in from Defender for Identity end up in the same incident instead of two separate alerts.

    • It all lives in the Microsoft Defender portal, which is also where Microsoft Sentinel is moving.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

docs.title: Microsoft Sentinel
docs.text:
• Microsoft Sentinel is a SIEM (security information and event management, a tool an organization uses to collect, analyze, and run security operations on its systems) and a SOAR (security orchestration, automation, and response, which coordinates and automates tasks between people and tools in one platform). It's cloud native and pulls in other Azure services to do its job.

  • It collects security data across your whole environment, detects threats, helps you investigate incidents (with AI help), and responds with automation.

  • Sentinel lives in the Microsoft Defender portal now. After March 31, 2027, it won't be supported in the Azure portal at all, and anyone still using it there gets redirected to Defender. New customers since July 2025 already get onboarded straight to the Defender portal.

  • Main features

    • Data connectors: connect to a bunch of data sources, Microsoft and third party.

    • Analytics rules: analyze your data and create alerts and incidents for suspicious activity.

    • Workbooks: dashboards built on Azure Monitor workbooks. Every tile in a workbook is just a KQL query underneath.

    • Automation: automation rules and playbooks. Playbooks are built on Azure Logic Apps.

    • Hunting: go looking for threats in your data before an alert ever fires.

    • Notebooks: Jupyter notebooks for deeper analysis. With the Sentinel data lake you can also run them from VS Code.

    • It's built on top of a Log Analytics workspace that holds all the data. Data connectors send data into the workspace first, and everything else queries it from there.

  • You query everything with KQL (Kusto Query Language).

  • Alerts come from analytics rules. You can start from Microsoft's rule templates (they come with solutions in the Content hub) or write your own.

  • Rule types

    • Scheduled: the most common one. A KQL query runs on a schedule over a lookback window and creates an alert if the results pass a threshold.

    • NRT (near-real-time): a limited kind of scheduled rule that runs every minute.

    • Anomaly: uses machine learning to learn a baseline and flag behavior outside of it. You can't edit the built-in ones, but you can duplicate one, tune it in Flighting mode, and compare it against the original. Anomalies don't create alerts on their own, they go to the Anomalies table so you can use them in hunting and other rules.

    • Microsoft security: creates Sentinel incidents from alerts in other Microsoft security products.

    • Threat intelligence: matches your logs against Microsoft's threat intel indicators. Only one rule allowed.

    • Fusion (advanced multistage attack detection): correlates lots of low-fidelity alerts into one high-fidelity incident. Logic is hidden and only one rule is allowed.

    • ML behavior analytics: Microsoft's own machine learning for weird SSH and RDP logins. Logic is hidden and not customizable.

What changes in the Defender portal

Once Sentinel is onboarded to the Defender portal (or Defender XDR incident integration is on), the Microsoft security rules and Fusion rules get turned off. Defender XDR creates and correlates the incidents instead. Microsoft is also pushing custom detections as the main way to write new rules across Sentinel and Defender XDR.

Documentation | Microsoft Learn

Documentation | Microsoft Learn - Types of analytics rules

Documentation | Microsoft Learn - Sentinel in the Defender portal

docs.title: Securing Data and Applications in Microsoft Azure
docs.text:
1. In an Azure SQL Database, when audit logs get written to a storage account, what blob type do they use?

    Append blobs

  2. You have an app on Azure App Service with its data in an Azure SQL Database. The database stores confidential employee data and you followed the best practices to secure it. You need to know about any attempt to steal data from the database right away. What do you do?

    Turn on Microsoft Defender for SQL (this used to be called Advanced Data Security) and set up alerts for the database.

  3. You need to turn on SQL database auditing. On which two levels can you define an auditing policy?

    Server level and database level

  4. What's the difference between a standard and a wildcard certificate?

    A standard certificate covers one domain. A wildcard certificate covers all the subdomains under one domain (like *.contoso.com).

  5. Which column encryption type supports equality lookups, joins, and group by in Azure SQL Database?

    Deterministic encryption (Always Encrypted). It always turns the same value into the same encrypted value, which is what makes the lookups work. The downside is someone might guess values by looking at patterns, especially if there are only a few possible values like True/False.
